scenario_reference.text: An application submits events that require the framework's event-processing services during normal operation, and the framework processes them completely and exactly as required; response measure unspecified.

analysis_records.stimulus: An application submits events that require the framework's event-processing services.
analysis_records.response_measure: unspecified: no response measure is supplied in the inputs for this scenario
architectural_decisions: Events are held in an Event Queue component (evidence: AE-5)
The Event Manager interacts directly with application handlers (evidence: AE-4)
A base Handler component is extended by standard handlers and application-specific handlers (evidence: AE-6)
The architecture is documented with class diagrams, component descriptions and defined component interactions (evidence: AE-1)
analysis_records.reasoning: Events pass through the Event Queue to the Event Manager, which invokes handlers derived from a common base Handler, so the architecture gives one defined path for event processing. The supplied material does not describe how the Event Manager selects the handler for a given event, nor what happens to an event for which no handler exists. No response measure is supplied, so whether processing is complete and exactly as required cannot be determined.

risks.description: Whether every submitted event reaches a handler that processes it as required is unresolved, because the handler-selection mechanism of the Event Manager is not described.
risks.rationale: The Event Manager calls application handlers directly and handlers are specializations of a base Handler, but the inputs do not state how an event is mapped to a handler or how unmatched events are treated; completeness of event processing therefore cannot be established from the supplied material.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Handler-selection and dispatch logic of the Event Manager toward application handlers

scenario_reference.text: Several events arrive one after another while the system is running with its single Event Queue and Event Manager, and the Event Manager dispatches them to their handlers in First-Come-First-Served order; response measure unspecified.

analysis_records.environment: Normal operation with a single Event Queue and a single Event Manager.
analysis_records.stimulus: Several events arrive one after another.
analysis_records.response_measure: unspecified: no response measure is supplied in the inputs for this scenario
architectural_decisions: Events are dispatched First-Come-First-Served (FIFO) (evidence: AE-9)
The architecture is limited to one Event Manager and one Event Queue (evidence: AE-14, AE-15)
Execution is on a single processor with sequential event processing (evidence: AE-8)
Events are held in an Event Queue component (evidence: AE-5)
analysis_records.reasoning: With exactly one Event Queue served by exactly one Event Manager on a single processor, there is a single point at which arrival order is recorded and a single consumer that removes events, so First-Come-First-Served dispatch follows from the structure. The same structure serializes all event processing, which ties the ordering guarantee to throughput. No response measure is supplied, so the scenario is judged only on whether the structure supports FIFO ordering, not on any timing target.

non_risks.description: FIFO dispatch order is supported by the structure: one queue, one Event Manager and sequential processing leave no second consumer that could reorder events.
non_risks.rationale: The FIFO constraint, the limit of one Event Queue and one Event Manager, and sequential single-processor execution are all stated in the inputs; together they mean events are removed and dispatched in arrival order. This is reasoned from the structure, not from a test result.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Dispatch ordering policy of the single Event Queue (FIFO)

tradeoff_points.parameter: Single Event Queue served sequentially by a single Event Manager on one processor
conflicting_attributes: Performance (all events serialized behind one consumer)

scenario_reference.text: No input has been received after the system has started, and the system remains in an idle wait state and resumes event processing when input arrives; response measure unspecified.

analysis_records.environment: The system has started and is awaiting input via the CLI.
analysis_records.response_measure: unspecified: no response measure is supplied in the inputs for this scenario
architectural_decisions: The system maintains an idle wait state until input is received (evidence: AE-10)
The system accepts input via a Command Line Interface (evidence: AE-7)
The Main module is part of the framework (evidence: AE-3)
analysis_records.reasoning: The framework, which owns the Main module, waits in an idle state until CLI input arrives, which corresponds directly to the stated idle-wait constraint. The supplied material does not describe how received CLI input is turned into an event and placed in the Event Queue, so the resumption half of the scenario is not traceable to a described mechanism. No response measure is supplied, so the time to resume processing cannot be assessed.

risks.description: How the system leaves the idle wait state and turns CLI input into queued events is not described, so whether processing resumes correctly when input arrives is unresolved.
risks.rationale: The idle-wait requirement and CLI input are stated, and the Main module belongs to the framework, but no component is identified as converting input into events for the Event Queue; the idle state is documented while the resume path is not.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Blocking idle wait on CLI input inside the framework-owned Main control loop

scenario_reference.text: A request to terminate the system is received during normal operation, and the STOP handler handles it and terminates the system; response measure unspecified.

analysis_records.stimulus: A request to terminate the system is received.
analysis_records.response_measure: unspecified: no response measure is supplied in the inputs for this scenario
architectural_decisions: A base Handler component is extended by standard handlers and application-specific handlers (evidence: AE-6)
Events are held in an Event Queue component (evidence: AE-5)
Events are dispatched First-Come-First-Served (FIFO) (evidence: AE-9)
analysis_records.reasoning: Termination is required to be handled by a STOP handler, and the architecture provides standard handlers derived from a base Handler, so a STOP handler fits the handler extension structure. The inputs do not say whether the STOP handler is one of the standard handlers, nor what happens to events still in the Event Queue when termination is requested. No response measure is supplied, so orderly termination cannot be assessed against a criterion.

risks.description: Whether termination via the STOP handler is orderly, for example what happens to events remaining in the Event Queue, is unresolved.
risks.rationale: The STOP-handler constraint and the handler hierarchy are stated, but neither the STOP handler's place in that hierarchy nor the treatment of pending queued events on termination is described; with FIFO dispatch a STOP event can be preceded or followed by other queued events whose fate is not stated.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Position of the STOP event in the single FIFO queue relative to pending events

scenario_reference.text: A failure occurs in a framework component during event processing in normal operation, and the system recovers and resumes event processing immediately; response measure unspecified ('immediate' is not quantified).

analysis_records.environment: Normal operation on a single processor with one Event Manager and one Event Queue.
analysis_records.stimulus: A failure occurs in a framework component during event processing.
analysis_records.response_measure: unspecified: 'immediate' recovery is not quantified in the inputs
architectural_decisions: The architecture is limited to one Event Manager and one Event Queue (evidence: AE-14, AE-15)
Execution is on a single processor with sequential event processing (evidence: AE-8)
Application logic is embedded within framework components (evidence: AE-11)
Application logic and the framework are highly inter-dependent (evidence: AE-2)
analysis_records.reasoning: The architecture has exactly one Event Manager and one Event Queue on a single processor, and application logic is embedded within framework components. The supplied material does not describe fault detection, redundancy, restart, or persistence of the Event Queue, so it cannot be established how the system would recover from a failure of either single element, or whether queued events survive. Because application code is embedded in framework components, a fault in application logic may affect framework components as well, and no fault-isolation boundary is described. 'Immediate' recovery is not quantified, so attainment cannot be determined.

risks.description: The single Event Manager and single Event Queue are potential single points of failure, and recovery after their failure is unresolved.
risks.rationale: The limits of one Event Manager and one Event Queue on a single processor are stated; the supplied material does not describe a redundant element, restart mechanism or queue persistence, so whether event processing can resume, and whether queued events are retained, cannot be determined.

risks.description: A fault in application logic may propagate into framework components, because the two are not separated.
risks.rationale: Application logic is embedded within framework components and the two are described as highly inter-dependent; no fault-isolation mechanism between application and framework code is described, so containment of an application-level failure is unresolved.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Number of Event Manager and Event Queue instances (fixed at 1)

tradeoff_points.parameter: Limit of one Event Manager and one Event Queue
conflicting_attributes: Conceptual Integrity (single, simple execution model and ordering)
Reliability (no redundant element to take over on failure)

risks.rationale: CLI input and the standard/application handler structure are stated, but no component is identified as validating input or handling user errors; whether erroneous input could reach the Event Queue or stop the processing loop cannot be determined from the supplied material.

architectural_decisions: The architecture is documented with class diagrams, component descriptions and defined component interactions (evidence: AE-1)
The Main module is part of the framework (evidence: AE-3)

The Event Manager interacts directly with application handlers (evidence: AE-4)

However, the class diagrams and interaction definitions themselves are not part of the supplied inputs, and application logic is embedded in framework components, so coordination also depends on application code respecting that contract. risks.rationale: The inputs state that interactions are defined but supply only a prose summary; with application logic embedded in framework components and direct manager-to-handler calls, coordination depends on details that the evaluation cannot inspect.

non_risks.description: Interaction between the Event Manager and handlers follows one uniform contract, because every handler derives from the same base Handler and control is owned by the framework.
non_risks.rationale: The base Handler extended by all standard and application-specific handlers, the framework-owned Main module and the documented component interactions together give a single interaction pattern for the Event Manager to invoke; this is reasoned from the described structure.

scenario_reference.text: Events of the same kind are submitted at different times during normal operation, and the architecture handles them with consistent behavior; response measure unspecified.

analysis_records.environment: Normal operation with sequential event processing.
analysis_records.stimulus: Events of the same kind are submitted at different times.
analysis_records.response_measure: unspecified: no response measure is supplied in the inputs for this scenario
architectural_decisions: Events are dispatched First-Come-First-Served (FIFO) (evidence: AE-9)
Execution is on a single processor with sequential event processing (evidence: AE-8)
The architecture is limited to one Event Manager and one Event Queue (evidence: AE-14, AE-15)
A base Handler component is extended by standard handlers and application-specific handlers (evidence: AE-6)
Application logic is embedded within framework components (evidence: AE-11)
analysis_records.reasoning: Sequential FIFO processing through one queue and one Event Manager means events of the same kind always pass through the same path in arrival order, with no concurrent interleaving. Whether the outcome is consistent also depends on handler state carried between events and on application-specific handlers overriding standard behaviour, neither of which is described. No response measure is supplied.

risks.description: Consistency of behaviour for repeated events of the same kind is unresolved where handlers keep state between events or application-specific handlers override standard behaviour.
risks.rationale: Application logic is embedded in framework components and application-specific handlers extend the base Handler, but the supplied material does not describe handler state or override rules, so whether the same event yields the same behaviour at different times cannot be determined.

non_risks.description: Processing order and execution path for events of the same kind are deterministic, because there is one queue, one Event Manager and sequential FIFO processing.
non_risks.rationale: With a single consumer and no concurrent execution, events cannot be reordered or interleaved, which removes concurrency as a source of inconsistent behaviour; this is reasoned from the stated structure and constraints.

scenario_reference.text: A new demand on system functionality arises during development or maintenance, and the new application-specific functionality is added to the architecture; response measure unspecified.

analysis_records.stimulus: A new demand on system functionality arises.
analysis_records.response_measure: unspecified: no response measure is supplied in the inputs for this scenario
architectural_decisions: A base Handler component is extended by standard handlers and application-specific handlers (evidence: AE-6)
Application logic is embedded within framework components (evidence: AE-11)
Application logic and the framework are highly inter-dependent (evidence: AE-2)
The Event Manager interacts directly with application handlers (evidence: AE-4)
analysis_records.reasoning: New application-specific functionality that can be expressed as event handling can be added as a new application-specific handler extending the base Handler, which localizes that kind of change. Functionality that does not fit a handler, or that touches application logic embedded within framework components, would require changing framework components, and the inter-dependence between application and framework makes the extent of such changes uncertain. No effort or time bound is supplied, so the cost of an addition cannot be determined.

risks.description: New functionality that is not a pure handler extension is likely to require changes to framework components, with an extent that cannot be determined.
risks.rationale: Application logic is embedded within framework components and application and framework are highly inter-dependent, so changes to application behaviour can reach into the framework; without representative change requests the size of that ripple is unknown.

non_risks.description: Adding a new event-handling behaviour as an application-specific handler has an explicit extension point.
non_risks.rationale: The base Handler is already extended by application-specific handlers, so a new handler subclass is an established way to add application functionality without altering the base; this is reasoned from the described structure.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Granularity of the base Handler extension point (what behaviour can be added by subclassing alone)

tradeoff_points.parameter: Direct interaction between the Event Manager and application handlers, without an intermediate dispatch layer
conflicting_attributes: Performance (fewer components per transaction, the stated performance proxy)
Modifiability (the manager depends directly on application handlers)
Variability (harder to substitute or add applications)

risks.description: Framework modifications are likely to propagate into application code because of the tight application-framework coupling, which threatens fast, cost-effective modification.
risks.rationale: The inputs state that application logic and framework are highly inter-dependent, that application logic is embedded within framework components and that the Event Manager calls application handlers directly; these increase the number of places a change can touch, though the actual effort cannot be determined without a change budget.

scenario_reference.text: A user submits input that generates an event during normal operation with sequential processing on a single processor, and the system processes the operation at the fastest possible speed; response measure unspecified ('fastest possible speed' is not quantified).

analysis_records.environment: Normal operation with sequential event processing on a single processor.
analysis_records.stimulus: A user submits input that generates an event.
analysis_records.response_measure: unspecified: 'fastest possible speed' is not quantified in the inputs
architectural_decisions: Performance is characterized by the number of components involved in a transaction, and transaction speed is described qualitatively as slow because of that number (evidence: AE-12, AE-13)
Execution is on a single processor with sequential event processing (evidence: AE-8)
Events are dispatched First-Come-First-Served (FIFO) (evidence: AE-9)
The architecture is limited to one Event Manager and one Event Queue (evidence: AE-14, AE-15)
The Event Manager interacts directly with application handlers (evidence: AE-4)
The system accepts input via a Command Line Interface (evidence: AE-7)
analysis_records.reasoning: Each event passes through several components (input, queue, manager, handler), and the inputs characterize transaction speed qualitatively as slow because of the number of components involved. All events are processed sequentially by one Event Manager from one FIFO queue, so a long-running handler delays every later event. 'Fastest possible speed' is not a measurable target, and no workload, benchmark or response-time target is supplied, so whether the scenario's response is attained cannot be determined; the findings below are potential latency risks only.

risks.description: Potential latency risk from the number of components involved per transaction.
risks.rationale: The inputs use component count per transaction as the performance proxy and describe transaction speed qualitatively as slow for that reason; no workload, benchmark or response-time target is supplied, so the actual latency impact cannot be determined.

risks.description: Potential head-of-line blocking: one slow handler delays all subsequent events in the single FIFO queue.
risks.rationale: Sequential processing on a single processor with one Event Manager and one FIFO queue means events wait for every earlier event to finish; whether this matters cannot be determined without a workload and a response-time target.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Number of components involved in an event transaction
Sequential, single-processor dispatch from one FIFO queue

gaps.missing_evidence: The class diagrams and component interaction descriptions referenced by the documentation status.
gaps.resolution_question: Can the class diagrams and interaction definitions be supplied for the evaluation?

gaps.description: No fault-isolation boundary between application logic embedded in framework components and the framework itself is described, so containment of application-level faults (REL-1) cannot be assessed.
gaps.missing_evidence: A description of how exceptions or failures in application handlers or embedded application logic are caught and contained.
gaps.resolution_question: If an application handler or embedded application logic fails, what happens to the Event Manager and the rest of the framework?

gaps.description: Whether the limit of one Event Manager and one Event Queue is a fixed design decision or a configurable parameter is not stated; this affects REL-1, VAR-2 and VAR-3.
gaps.missing_evidence: The rationale for the one-manager, one-queue limit and whether it can be changed.
gaps.resolution_question: Is the limit of one Event Manager and one Event Queue intended to be permanent, or can more instances be configured?

gaps.description: No mechanism for registering, distinguishing or isolating several applications using the framework at the same time is described (VAR-3).
gaps.missing_evidence: A description of how applications attach to the framework and how their handlers and events are kept apart.
gaps.resolution_question: Is the framework intended to serve more than one application at once, and if so how are applications attached and isolated?

gaps.description: Whether handlers keep state between events, and the rules by which application-specific handlers may override standard handler behaviour, are not described, which limits the analysis of consistent behaviour (CI-2).
gaps.missing_evidence: Handler lifecycle and state description, and the override rules of the handler hierarchy.
gaps.resolution_question: Are handlers stateless across events, and which standard behaviour may application-specific handlers override?
